scope: Generate testable relationships among modern cognitive/biomedical evidence, phenomenology, cultural interpretation, social roles, and historical institutional responses without retrospective diagnosis.

modern prevalence can be projected into historical populations

hypotheses.title: Societies may differentially channel people with unusual experiential or cognitive profiles into specialist roles, stigma, or exclusion
discriminating_evidence: trait measures before intensive training where possible
hypotheses.historical_rule: Historical descriptions may be coded as traits/experiences only when source-bounded. They cannot be converted into a modern diagnosis.

hypotheses.title: Large-scale witch-hunting is better modeled through ideational, institutional and network diffusion than through presumed neurological traits of accused persons

supporting_candidates.title: Ideational diffusion and the great witch hunt in Central Europe
supporting_candidates.authors: Kerice Doten-Snitker, Steven Pfaff, Yuan Hsiao
supporting_candidates.use: Models print diffusion, nearby trials and contextual variables as mechanisms of persecution spread.

supporting_candidates.title: Witchcraft or Mycotoxin? The Salem Witch Trials
supporting_candidates.use: Adversarial check on a famous biomedical/environmental monocausal account; concludes ergotism is unlikely to explain much of Salem.

discriminating_evidence: trial-level person data linked to city/network timing
negative-control regions with witch beliefs but few trials

publication_rule: No hypothesis in this file is an approved NOEMA claim. Cross-domain historical transport requires explicit human review and rival-model testing.
